title: What is Democracy?
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about how the idea of "rule by the people" grew from ancient Athens into the modern democracies of the English-speaking world -- and what it takes to keep it alive.
competenceGoals: discuss and elaborate on political systems in English-speaking countries and compare with the Norwegian system
explain the main features of democratic governance and citizens' rights

content.content:
## Imagine a country where you have no say

Picture this: tomorrow, every decision about your life -- what you can say online, what you learn in school, who runs your town -- is made by a handful of people you never chose and cannot remove. You have no vote, no court to appeal to, no newspaper free to criticise them. For much of human history, and for many people still today, this was simply normal.

Now think of the alternative we so often take for granted. The word *democracy* comes from two ancient Greek words: *demos*, meaning the people, and *kratos*, meaning power or rule. Put them together and you get "rule by the people." It sounds simple, almost obvious. Yet behind that little word lies one of the boldest experiments humans have ever attempted -- the idea that ordinary people should shape the laws that govern their own lives.

Democracy is far more than dropping a ballot in a box every few years. It rests on a set of promises: that leaders answer to the people, that everyone counts equally, and that even those who lose a vote keep their fundamental rights. As you read this chapter, keep one question in mind, the same one that has occupied thinkers for centuries: what actually makes a government *truly* democratic?

## Five promises every democracy makes

If you asked a hundred political scientists to define democracy, most would point to the same core principles -- and once you know them, you can hold any government up to the light and ask how well it measures up.

The first is **popular sovereignty**: the government's authority comes from the consent of the governed, expressed through regular, free, and fair elections. The second is **political equality**, captured in the phrase "one person, one vote" -- your voice counts the same whether you are rich or poor, whatever your gender, ethnicity or background. The third is the **rule of law**: laws apply to everyone, including those in power, and no one stands above them. The fourth is the **protection of rights and freedoms** -- speech, press, religion, peaceful assembly -- usually written into a constitution or bill of rights. And the fifth is **majority rule with minority rights**: decisions follow the majority, but the majority is never allowed to trample the basic rights of those who think differently.

These ideas have a long history. Democracy first appeared in ancient Athens around 508 BCE, under reforms led by Cleisthenes. Athenian democracy was *direct* -- citizens gathered on a hill called the Pnyx to debate and vote on laws themselves, and many offices were filled by lottery rather than election so that wealth could not dominate. But "citizen" was a narrow category: women, enslaved people and foreigners were excluded, so perhaps only ten to twenty percent of the population could take part. The democracy we know today -- *representative* democracy, where we elect others to decide on our behalf -- developed much later, shaped by Enlightenment thinkers such as John Locke, Montesquieu and Jean-Jacques Rousseau, and given living form in the American and French revolutions of 1776 and 1789. Switzerland today blends the two, putting major questions to citizens in national referendums while still electing a government for daily affairs.

exercise.task: Test yourself on the foundations of democracy:

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: What do the Greek roots of the word "democracy" mean?

options.text: "Rule by the people"
"Rule by the wise"
"Rule by the wealthy"
"Rule of law"

questions.solution: *Demos* means the people and *kratos* means power or rule, so democracy literally means rule by the people.

questions.task: Which principle protects those who lose a vote from having their basic freedoms stripped away?

options.text: Popular sovereignty
Majority rule with minority rights
Political equality
The rule of law

questions.solution: Majority rule with minority rights means the majority decides, but it cannot vote away the fundamental rights of the minority.

questions.task: How did democracy in ancient Athens differ from democracy in modern Norway or the UK?

options.text: Athens excluded no one from voting
Athens used proportional representation
Athens was direct, with citizens voting on laws themselves
Athens had no concept of citizenship

questions.solution: Athenian democracy was direct -- eligible citizens debated and voted on laws in person -- though it excluded women, enslaved people and foreigners. Modern democracies are mainly representative.

questions.task: What does the principle of "rule of law" require?

options.text: That the most popular leader can change any law
That courts always side with the government
That only judges may vote
That laws apply to everyone, including those in power

questions.solution: The rule of law means laws apply equally to all, and no one -- not even the powerful -- stands above them.

content.content:
## The machinery that keeps power honest

Promises are not enough on their own; democracies need machinery to make them real. The most important piece is the **separation of powers**. Most democracies split government authority into three branches that watch one another. The **legislative** branch -- parliament or congress -- makes the laws. The **executive** branch -- a president or prime minister and cabinet -- carries them out. The **judicial** branch -- the courts -- interprets the laws and checks that they fit the constitution. By dividing power this way, no single person or group can gather it all up. In Norway, for instance, the Storting makes law, the government implements it, and independent courts can strike down a law that breaks the constitution.

Elections are the heartbeat of this system, but only if they are genuinely **free** (no coercion), **fair** (a level playing field for all parties), **transparent** (counted in the open) and **periodic** (held at regular intervals). Around this core sits a wider ecosystem: an independent press that acts as a watchdog, investigating and reporting on those in power; a lively civil society of unions, charities and campaign groups through which citizens organise; and constitutional protections that set out the rules of the game and guarantee citizens' rights. The United Kingdom has no single written constitution, relying instead on a body of law and convention, yet the same protective function is there.

Notice the comparison threading through all of this. Norway is a constitutional monarchy with proportional representation and a strong welfare tradition; the United States is a presidential republic; the UK is a parliamentary monarchy. They differ in structure, but each rests on the same five promises. And none of them is finished. Every democracy faces pressures -- low turnout, the influence of money, the spread of misinformation -- which is why democracy is best understood not as a thing you *have* but as a project you keep working on.

options.text: placeholder

questions.task: Why do democracies separate power into legislative, executive and judicial branches?

options.text: So that no single person or group can hold all the power
To make government slower on purpose
To give the courts control over elections
To remove the need for a constitution

questions.solution: The separation of powers spreads authority across branches that check one another, so power cannot be concentrated and abused.

questions.task: Which of these is essential for an election to count as genuinely democratic?

options.text: It is held only once a generation
It is free, fair, transparent and held at regular intervals
Only the governing party may field candidates
The results are kept secret from the public

questions.solution: Genuinely democratic elections must be free, fair, transparent and periodic -- otherwise voting becomes a facade.

questions.task: In what sense does the text describe the press as a "watchdog"?

options.text: It reports only good news about the government
It replaces the courts
It investigates those in power and holds them accountable
It is controlled by the executive branch

questions.solution: A free press acts as a watchdog, scrutinising and reporting on those in power so citizens can hold them to account.

questions.task: How does the chapter suggest we should think about democracy?

options.text: As a finished system that needs no maintenance
As something only ancient societies achieved
As identical in structure in every country
As an ongoing project that must be defended and improved

questions.solution: Democracy is presented as an ongoing project facing constant pressures, not a fixed state -- which is why engaged citizens matter.

content.content:
## In short

Democracy means rule by the people, and it rests on five promises: popular sovereignty, political equality, the rule of law, the protection of rights and freedoms, and majority rule tempered by minority rights. It was born in ancient Athens as a *direct* democracy and reshaped by Enlightenment thinkers into the *representative* democracies we know today, where we elect others to decide for us. To keep those promises, democracies rely on the separation of powers, free and fair elections, an independent press and constitutional protections. Norway, the UK and the US share these foundations while differing in form. No democracy is perfect or permanent -- which is exactly why understanding it, and taking part in it, matters.
